e.t: This word is a proper name rendered “Aarōnidēs” or “Aaronithis.” It functions as a name rather than as a general description, so its central meaning is identification of the person or group bearing that name. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:12. The available word-level information establishes the name and its naming function, but the reference alone does not provide enough verse text to explain the specific person or significance intended there.

This adverb means “as befits a brother”: it describes something done in a manner appropriate to, or characteristic of, a brother. It tells the reader how an action is carried out rather than naming the action itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 4 Maccabees 10:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea is conduct fitting a brotherly relationship.

This Greek LXX verb means “sing praise.” It describes the act of expressing praise, especially in worship or song. The word is used broadly across the Greek Old Testament and related writings, appearing 119 times in this LXX corpus. Its central idea remains active praise rather than merely holding admiration inwardly. The surrounding verse determines who is praised and how the praise is expressed.

This verb means to be unfortunate or to experience an unfavorable condition. It describes a person or situation marked by hardship or poor fortune, rather than naming a specific event or action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 14:8. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly how the word functions there, but its basic sense is being unfortunate.

This word means “like a grove,” describing something associated with or resembling a group of trees. It can function as an adjective, identifying a grove-like quality, or as a noun referring to something grove-like. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times in seven verses, including passages in 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its central image is therefore a wooded or grove-like place or feature, while the precise sense in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This LXX word means “at once” or “together.” As an adverb, it can describe actions happening simultaneously or people and things occurring in company with one another. As a preposition, it can connect someone or something with another person or thing. The word appears 108 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so its basic idea is used broadly: joining, accompanying, or happening at the same time. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on simultaneity or being together.

Amessa is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is a name rather than a descriptive word that states an action, quality, or relationship. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in two verses: once in 1 Kings 2:32 and twice in 1 Chronicles 2:17. Without the surrounding verse text, no further personal description should be attached to the name itself.

gl: act bravely; behave in a manly way
d: act bravely; behave in a manly way

e.t: This verb means to act bravely or to behave in a manly way. It describes courageous conduct, emphasizing what a person does rather than merely what that person is. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Maccabees 16:23, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word therefore points to brave, resolute behavior in action.

This word means a flower, referring to the bloom or visible flowering part of a plant. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings to name flowers in both literal descriptions and comparisons. The word occurs 26 times across 25 verses, showing that it is a recurring everyday image in this corpus rather than a rare term. Its central meaning remains simple: a flower, whether mentioned as part of a plant, an ornament, or a picture of life’s beauty and brevity.

This noun means “transcript”: a written copy or reproduced document. It names something put into writing so that its contents can be preserved, delivered, or consulted as an official record. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 18 times, especially in Esther and 1 Maccabees, where its use belongs to written administrative or public communication. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

gl: not to be moved by prayer; inexorable
d: not to be moved by prayer; inexorable

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something that cannot be persuaded or turned aside by pleading: “not to be moved by prayer; inexorable.” It presents firmness that does not yield to appeals. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in the Wisdom of Solomon. The word focuses on an unyielding response rather than simply describing strength or persistence. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and the person or thing being described.

gl: settlement far from home; colony settlement
d: settlement far from home; colony settlement

e.t: This noun refers to a settlement established far from the homeland—a colony or community of people living away from their original country. It can describe the settlement itself rather than merely the journey or condition of being away. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, the word occurs 31 times, especially in Jeremiah and Ezra, where it is associated with people living away from their native land or with communities formed in another place. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

gl: let fall drop by drop; distil
d: let fall drop by drop; distil

e.t: This Greek Old Testament verb means “let fall drop by drop” or “distil.” It describes liquid released gradually in drops rather than poured out all at once. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, chiefly in Proverbs and once in Song of Songs. Its uses are associated with images of something flowing or being expressed in small drops, while the surrounding verse determines the exact picture. It is a verb, so it describes the action of dripping or distilling.

This verb means “split,” describing the act of separating something into distinct parts or moving people apart. It is an action word rather than a name or description of an object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within the Old Testament corpus: twice in Numbers and once in 2 Chronicles. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being separated and the surrounding sentence. The basic idea remains straightforward: to divide or separate rather than leave something joined together.

This noun means “chief baker,” referring to the person who held that position in a royal household. It identifies an official baker rather than describing baking as an action. In the Greek Old Testament, the term occurs seven times, all in Genesis, in the account involving Pharaoh’s household and its servants. Its central meaning remains a title for a baker with recognized authority or rank.

Asōnaios is a proper name, also rendered Asoneos. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, at 2 Samuel 23:8. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide a broader common-word meaning. Because it is a personal name, readers should not treat it as a general word carrying a separate moral or theological definition. Its precise significance there depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This Greek LXX noun means “ill-luck” or “misfortune”—an unfavorable condition or bad outcome that happens to someone. It names adversity or disappointing circumstances rather than an action a person performs. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains bad fortune or an unfortunate situation.

Baithanabra, also rendered “Vethanavra,” is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named location or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Joshua 13:27. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its specific geographic significance cannot be explained further here; the lexical evidence establishes it primarily as the name Baithanabra.

This Greek LXX adverb means “hardly.” It qualifies an action or statement by showing that something is difficult, limited, or only barely true. In ordinary English, it draws attention to how little, how rarely, or with how much difficulty something occurs, depending on the sentence. It appears five times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Genesis, Isaiah, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This verb means “hurt”: it describes causing pain, injury, or damage to a person or thing. As an action word, it presents hurting as something done, rather than naming the person affected or the injury itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in Proverbs, Wisdom, and Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being hurt and the surrounding sentence.

Boula, also rendered Vula, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 19:4. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular role there cannot be explained further, but its lexical meaning is limited to the name itself.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Gennaios” or “Yenneos.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs 12 times, all in the deuterocanonical books, especially 4 Maccabees. The precise person identified depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a proper name.

Golon is a proper name—a personal or place name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 36:23. The available meaning is therefore the name itself: “Gōlōn” or “Golon.” Its precise identification and significance depend on the surrounding genealogical context, which is not included here. This LXX word should be understood as a distinct Greek rendering of a named entity, not as a general vocabulary term.

This verb means “escape notice.” It describes something happening without coming to another person’s attention or recognition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 4:6, so its basic meaning is clear even though its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word focuses on remaining unnoticed rather than on the action itself, and it can describe an event or act that does not become known to those present.

This Greek LXX noun means “division.” It names a separating or dividing of something into distinct portions, groups, or parts. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Ezekiel and Micah. Its basic sense is straightforward: it points to the fact or result of things being divided rather than remaining together. The surrounding verse determines what is divided and how the division functions in context.

This word refers to an interlude or a pause for rest. As a noun, it marks a break within a song or poetic passage, allowing the reader or singer to pause before continuing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 76 times, almost always in Psalms, and also appears in Habakkuk. Its placement in these writings indicates a musical or poetic pause rather than an action, person, or spoken message. The exact force of the pause in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Engaddi is a proper name, referring to “Engaddi” rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. It appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, in two passages in 1 Samuel and once in Song of Songs. The name remains consistent in each recorded rendering, so its basic meaning is its identification of Engaddi. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “glue to”: to join something closely to another thing, as with adhesive. It describes attachment or being firmly joined rather than mere contact. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Zechariah 14:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself presents the action of being joined closely to something else.

This pronoun means “that,” pointing to a person, thing, or matter already identified or distinguished from others. It helps direct attention to a particular subject rather than naming the subject itself. Its exact reference depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 649 times, showing that it is a common way to identify or point out something specific.

This adjective describes someone as “out of one's mind” or “senseless,” pointing to behavior or thinking that lacks sound judgment. It functions as a description of a person’s condition or conduct, not as a title or personal name. The word occurs three times in the Greek text of 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains a serious departure from ordinary sense and reason.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “go out over; pass beyond.” It describes movement outward and across or beyond a boundary, rather than remaining within a place. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Numbers 11:31, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in that occurrence depends on how the sentence uses this movement verb.

This Greek LXX verb means “drained” or “exhausted,” describing something that has been emptied of strength, supply, or remaining substance. It expresses the action or condition of being completely spent rather than merely reduced or weakened. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Job 5:5, and is rendered “exhausted.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is clear: something has been used up or left without strength.

This Greek LXX verb means “roll up,” describing something being gathered or curled into a rolled form. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Job and Isaiah, so its normal sense is clear but its wider range of use is limited. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and imagery.

Elnaam is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary action, quality, or object word, so its main function is to name someone rather than describe what that person does. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 11:46. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify the person’s specific role or connection in that passage.

gl: preservation of life; maintenance of life
d: preservation of life; maintenance of life

e.t: This noun refers to the “preservation of life” or “maintenance of life.” It describes the sustaining and continuing of life, rather than life simply as a living being. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, all in deuterocanonical books, so its use is focused and relatively uncommon. Its central idea is life being kept or sustained. The precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

This verb means “have in” or “hold in.” It describes keeping something within oneself or retaining it, rather than simply possessing something externally. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs five times, so it is an uncommon word. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what is being held and the surrounding sentence. It appears in Genesis, 2 Kings, Ezekiel, and 3 Maccabees, showing that its basic idea is used across several biblical writings.

This noun means “insides,” referring to the inner parts of the body. It describes what is within a person rather than the outward appearance. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Genesis and twice in deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains the body’s inner parts.

This adverb means “all at once,” describing something that happens suddenly or in a single movement rather than gradually. It can mark an abrupt change, action, or event, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what occurs. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears 14 times, making it an established word for sudden, collective action or change. Its core meaning remains consistent across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books: something takes place all at once.

This Greek LXX verb means “despise”: to regard someone or something as unworthy of respect or consideration. It describes an active attitude or response rather than a person, object, or quality. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, across Jeremiah, Daniel, Amos, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but its central sense remains treating someone or something with contempt or disregard.

This noun means “enchantment,” referring to a spell or magical practice. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Deuteronomy and Isaiah, and its wording concerns practices associated with attempts to influence or affect matters through magic. The word names the practice itself rather than describing a person who performs it. Its precise force in either passage is understood from the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “travel on”: to proceed or continue moving from one place toward another. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, with occurrences in Leviticus, Ezekiel, 2 Maccabees, 3 Maccabees, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains movement onward or passage along a route.

This adverb describes something as “unstable,” conveying a lack of firmness, steadiness, or security. It tells how an action or condition exists rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 4:4; the surrounding verse text is not available, so its precise force there must be understood from that passage’s context. Its central idea remains instability or an unsteady condition.

This noun means "desert" or "wilderness": a desolate, uncultivated region rather than a settled place. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe an actual barren landscape, and it may also refer to land left empty or deserted. The word occurs nine times in eight verses, chiefly in Isaiah, with additional occurrences in Ezra and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a place marked by desolation, emptiness, or wildness.

This noun means “kindness of heart” and “considerateness”: a thoughtful, humane regard for another person. It describes an inward disposition that leads someone to treat others with care rather than hardness or disregard. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Esther 8:12. The word’s basic sense is clear from its definition, while the surrounding passage would determine how that kindness is expressed there.

This adjective describes something that is well shaded or shadowy. It points to the quality of being covered by shade or marked by shadow, rather than to an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 11:16. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wording, but the central idea remains a place or thing characterized by abundant shade or darkness.

Ēthir, also rendered Ithir, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific individual in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 25:28. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, Scripture does not provide enough information here to explain the person’s role or the significance of the name beyond identifying that individual.

Tharaba, also rendered Tharava, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Esther 1:10. Because the available information identifies it as a name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its specific identity or role there cannot be explained further from the word alone. Its meaning is therefore best presented as the personal name “Tharaba” or “Tharava.”

This word means “determination” or “will”—the desire, purpose, or decision that directs someone’s action. It is a noun describing what a person or another acting subject wants or intends. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 40 times, including passages in Psalms, Isaiah, and the historical books. English translations commonly render it as “will,” which fits its central sense of deliberate desire or purpose.

This verb means “make bold” or “embolden”—to give someone courage, confidence, or resolve to act. It describes strengthening another person so that fear or hesitation no longer controls the response. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 3 Maccabees, at 1:22 and 1:26. The exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains making someone bolder or more courageous.

This Greek LXX verb means “enthrone”: to place someone on a throne or establish that person in royal rule. It describes an action rather than a title, pointing to the formal elevation of a ruler. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Esther 1:2. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but its central meaning remains the placing of someone in the position of a king or sovereign.

This word means “healing”: the restoration of a person’s health or condition. It is a noun, naming the act or result of being made well rather than describing someone who heals. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 27 times, showing a recurring concern with recovery and restored well-being. Its use spans books such as Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Sirach. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains healing or restoration.

Iezebouth, also rendered Iezevuth, is a proper name preserved as a name rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 12:22. The available information identifies how the name is represented, but does not establish from the name alone whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise identification therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word refers to mud or slime: wet, soft material that can cling to or cover something. It is a noun, so it names the material itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms. Its basic sense remains concrete and physical; the surrounding verse determines how that material is being used in a particular passage.

Isia is a proper name, used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented as a common word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship, so its meaning is the personal name itself rather than an idea to define. In this LXX corpus, Isia occurs three times, in two verses of 1 Chronicles, and is rendered “Isia” each time. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding biblical passage.

This verb means to experience something bad or to suffer. It describes undergoing hardship or distress rather than causing harm to someone else. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jonah 4:10, and its basic sense is expressed as suffering. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific situation, but the word itself focuses on a person’s experience of something painful, difficult, or harmful.

gl: any kind of nut; flower of almond
d: any kind of nut; flower of almond

e.t: This Greek LXX noun refers to a nut, especially an almond or an almond blossom. It names the almond-related objects described in Exodus 25, where the word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus 25:33 and 25:34. Its basic meaning is botanical and concrete: a nut or the flower of an almond tree. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its particular role in either passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “look down at,” describing the act of directing one’s eyes downward toward something or someone. It expresses a visual action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, in Genesis 18:16, so its normal meaning is established from this single recorded occurrence. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its translation context.

This Greek LXX verb means “whirl down” or “lead astray.” It describes an action that either sends something downward in a sweeping or turbulent way, or causes someone to depart from the right path. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers 32:13. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense centers on downward movement or misdirection.

This Greek LXX verb means “overwhelm”: to overcome or overpower someone or something with force. It describes an action rather than a person, quality, or object. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Zechariah 9:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of overwhelming or overpowering. This is a distinct Greek LXX word and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament entry.

This adjective means “called” or “named.” It describes someone or something identified by a particular name or designation. As an adjective, it qualifies a person or thing rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament material represented here, it occurs three times, all in the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its exact force in any one sentence depends on what person or object it describes, but its central idea remains being called or designated by a name.

This Greek LXX noun means “strength”—the quality or source of being strong. It refers to strength as a real capacity, not an action or command. In this corpus, it occurs four times, all in the Psalms, where the wording repeatedly renders the term as “strength.” Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains firm ability, power, or support. The word appears in Psalms 24:14, 27:8, 30:4, and 42:2.

This Greek LXX noun refers to any loud noise or a crash—a sudden, forceful sound. It names the sound itself rather than an action or person. The word occurs once in the Greek text of the deuterocanonical book of Wisdom, at Wisdom 17:17. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, its exact force there cannot be described further, but its basic meaning remains a distinctly loud or crashing sound.

This adjective means “servile”: describing something connected with serving or the condition of a servant. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 13 times, all within the Old Testament portion of the Greek Septuagint. Its occurrences appear in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers, especially in instructions connected with appointed feast days and sacred assemblies. The word therefore identifies a service-related character or duty, while the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means “ransoming; redemption”: the act of securing someone’s release by paying the required price or providing the means of release. It can describe redemption in practical situations, such as the recovery of a person or property, and it is also used of God’s saving action. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, in eight verses. Its central idea is release from an obligation, bondage, or threatened loss through redemption.

Maeleth is a proper name, rendered “Maeleth.” It identifies a person, place, or title by name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Genesis and twice in Psalms. The available references are Genesis 28:9, Psalm 52:1, and Psalm 87:1. Without the surrounding verse text, the specific referent at each occurrence cannot be identified here, but the word’s basic function is clear: it is a named designation, not a descriptive word with a broader ordinary meaning.

Malouch, also rendered Malukh, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies individuals mentioned in Ezra and Nehemiah. The name appears six times across six verses, with two occurrences in Ezra and four in Nehemiah. Because the available passages do not include their verse text or surrounding context, the name’s particular family or role cannot be identified here. Its ordinary meaning in this corpus is therefore the proper name Malouch or Malukh.

Marōdach, also rendered Marothakh, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Isaiah and once in Jeremiah. Because no broader definition is given for this name, its meaning is best understood as the personal designation itself: “Marōdach; Marothakh.”

This LXX noun means “magnate,” referring to a person of high rank or importance. It is used as a title or description for prominent people rather than as an action or quality. The word occurs 30 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this LXX corpus, appearing in 30 verses. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding wording.

This verb means “beckon”: to signal or call someone to come nearer. It describes an action directed toward another person, inviting or drawing that person’s attention and approach. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Hosea 11:1–2. The word’s basic meaning remains simple and active: someone beckons another. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and its wording.

This verb means to change one’s abode or remove to another place. It describes a person leaving one residence and settling elsewhere, so its central idea is relocation rather than merely traveling briefly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 15:19. The word itself does not specify whether the move is voluntary, forced, temporary, or permanent; those details must come from the surrounding passage. Its basic focus remains the act of changing where one lives.

This noun means “one initiated”: a person who has been admitted or introduced into something. It identifies the person as the recipient of an initiating process, rather than naming the process itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Wisdom 12:5. The word’s precise significance in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a person who is initiated.

Naas is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a broader meaning; its function is personal identification. The name occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 11 verses, and is consistently rendered “Naas.” Its occurrences extend from 1 Samuel through 1 Chronicles, showing continued use of the same personal name in several historical books.

Nisa is a proper name, presented as the name “Nisa.” As a name, it identifies a particular person or named subject rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. This Greek LXX word occurs twice, both times in Esther: once in Esther 1:1 and once in Esther 8:9. The available lexical information does not provide a broader descriptive meaning or explain the name’s historical origin. Its precise reference in either passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage context.

e.h: A Brood or Group of Young
e.t: This Greek LXX noun means “brood,” referring to a group of young animals or birds belonging to a mother. It names the young collectively rather than one individual creature. The word occurs 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing a normal descriptive use for offspring gathered or considered as a group. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a brood: young creatures viewed together.

Oziēlis, also written Ozilis, is a proper name identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 3:27. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named there.

The word means an inhabitant: a person who lives in a particular place. It is a noun that identifies someone by residence, focusing on the fact that the person lives there rather than describing an action. In the Greek LXX, it occurs twice, once in Proverbs and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word means “hoof”: the hard covering at the end of an animal’s foot. It is a noun used to name this part of an animal, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times, with occurrences confined to Leviticus and Deuteronomy. For an ordinary reader, it points to the visible hoof itself—the part of the foot being named. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “get up at dawn.” It describes the action of rising early in the morning, before or as daylight begins. The word is used 54 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so its basic sense is a normal description of when someone rises, not a special title or abstract idea. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being described.

e.h: Play or Take Part in Play
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “play”: to engage in playful activity or take part in a game or amusement. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, with uses extending from Genesis through Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary sense remains the act of playing or engaging in playful activity.

This Greek LXX verb means “pose” or “serve”: it describes placing something before someone or presenting it for use. The same basic idea can extend naturally from setting an object in position to making something available or serving it. It occurs 31 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is used across a range of passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being placed or presented there.

This word means working to earn the necessities of life—laboring for one’s daily bread.
